name: Coherentism
statement: A belief is justified by cohering with a web of other beliefs, not by resting on foundations.
statementAccent: cohering with a web of other beliefs
meaning: Coherentism is a theory of epistemic justification holding that a belief is justified in virtue of belonging to, and cohering with, a system or web of other beliefs, rather than by resting on foundational beliefs. It is the chief rival to foundationalism. Where foundationalism pictures justified belief as a building resting on a base of basic beliefs, coherentism replaces that image with a web or raft in which each belief both supports and is supported by others, and no belief is intrinsically privileged or self-justifying. Justification, on this view, is holistic and mutual: a belief is justified not by being traced back to some special foundation but by how well it fits into the overall system of a person's beliefs. A classic image is Neurath's boat, the picture of a ship that must be rebuilt plank by plank while staying afloat at sea, with no dry dock and no foundation to stand on, capturing the idea that we revise our beliefs from within the web rather than from any external bedrock. Coherentism answers the regress problem differently from foundationalism: instead of stopping the regress at basic beliefs, it treats justification as a property of the whole interconnected system rather than a chain running back to a base. Coherence is understood to require more than mere logical consistency, involving explanatory and inferential connections among beliefs.
mechanism: Coherentism explains justification through relations of mutual support within a whole system of beliefs, rather than through support flowing one way from foundations. On the coherentist picture, there are no basic beliefs that are justified independently of all others; instead, each belief is justified by how it hangs together with the rest, and each part both supports and is supported by other parts, as in a web or a raft. This is why coherentism is called holistic: what is justified in the first instance is the whole system, and individual beliefs are justified derivatively by belonging to a coherent system. Coherentists take this to answer the regress problem by rejecting its linear assumption; faced with the trilemma of an infinite regress, a foundation, or a circle, coherentism embraces a non-vicious, holistic form of the circular option, where justification loops back through the system rather than terminating at a base. Crucially, coherence is more than logical consistency: a set of beliefs can be consistent yet incoherent if the beliefs are unrelated, so coherence additionally demands positive connections, explanatory relations, and inferential and probabilistic ties that knit the beliefs into an integrated whole. Laurence BonJour, in his influential 1985 defense, tried to spell out coherence in terms of features such as the number and strength of inferential connections among beliefs and the absence of division into unrelated subsystems, and gave beliefs close to experience a special role, though he later abandoned coherentism.

examples.text: Coherentism pictures justified belief as a web in which each belief supports and is supported by others, with no privileged foundation.
We rebuild our beliefs plank by plank while afloat, with no dry dock, as Neurath's image of the ship at sea suggests.
A set of unrelated beliefs can be consistent yet incoherent, so coherence demands explanatory and inferential connections.

variants.name: Holistic justification
variants.text: The view that the whole system of beliefs is justified in the first instance, individual beliefs deriving justification from it.

variants.name: BonJour's coherentism
variants.text: Laurence BonJour's 1985 account spelling out coherence and giving observational beliefs a role, later abandoned by him.

whyItMatters: Coherentism is one of the two dominant theories of the structure of epistemic justification, the principal alternative to foundationalism, and the debate between them is central to the theory of knowledge. By denying that justification must rest on a privileged base of basic beliefs, coherentism offers a distinctive answer to the ancient regress problem, replacing the foundationalist building with a web of mutually supporting beliefs and treating justification as a holistic property of the whole system. Its image of Neurath's boat, rebuilding the ship at sea with no dry dock, has become one of the most evocative pictures in epistemology, capturing the idea that we always reason from within our web of beliefs rather than from some external foundation. Coherentism draws on a rich tradition, from the British idealists Bradley and Bosanquet through Neurath, Hempel, and Quine's web of belief to contemporary defenders, and it forces foundationalists to say why any belief should count as basic. Even though it faces serious objections about its connection to reality, coherentism keeps alive the insight that beliefs are justified together, not one at a time.

working.text: deny that any belief is justified independently of all others, as foundationalism claims.
justify a belief by how well it coheres with the surrounding web of beliefs.
require more than consistency, seeking explanatory and inferential connections that integrate the beliefs.

limits: Coherentism faces two powerful objections that turn on its relation to experience and reality. The isolation, or input, objection holds that coherence alone can be cut off from the world: since justification is a matter of internal fit among beliefs, there seems to be no guarantee that a coherent system accurately reflects external reality, and a richly coherent but wholly false system, like a well-constructed fairy tale or a systematic delusion, could count as justified. The alternative-systems, or plurality, objection presses that many different, equally coherent but mutually incompatible systems of belief are possible, so coherence by itself cannot single out the true one or indicate truth. Both objections center on the role of experience and observation, and coherentists typically respond by giving perceptual or observational beliefs a special place in the system, which critics say risks smuggling foundationalism back in. There is also genuine disagreement about what coherence precisely consists in beyond mere consistency.
misreadings: Coherentism is not the claim that any consistent set of beliefs is justified; coherence requires more than logical consistency, demanding explanatory and inferential connections, and unrelated but consistent beliefs are not thereby coherent. It is not committed to circular reasoning in the vicious sense, since it rejects the linear picture and treats justification as a holistic property of the whole system. And it is not obviously cut off from reality by design, since coherentists give observational beliefs a role, though whether this succeeds is disputed, so treating coherentism as mere consistency, as viciously circular, or as ignoring experience, misreads the coherence theory of justification.
origin: A theory of the structure of epistemic justification holding that beliefs are justified by cohering with a whole system of beliefs rather than by resting on foundations, developed from the British idealists through Neurath, Quine, and BonJour.

sources.text: Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — coherentism as the view that justification is holistic and a matter of coherence within a system of beliefs rather than foundations, BonJour's 1985 account of coherence and the role of observational beliefs, and the isolation and alternative-systems objections.

Coherentism in Epistemology, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — coherence as mutual support in a web of beliefs, the contrast with foundationalism and the regress trilemma, the requirement that coherence exceed mere consistency, and the idealist and logical-empiricist figures associated with the view.
